title: Split the undeterminable CI case, and give an orphaned shipped commit a way back

history.detail:
PASS: PASS — round 1. Audited 7586ee2 with bookkeeping 9102c11, main checkout. Sprint file read fresh.

Neither FAIL trigger fired. Both were checked by construction and by running, and Req 3's was the one worth the time.

================================================================
REQ 3 — THE LAUNDERING PATH. ATTACKED, NOT CONFIRMED.
================================================================

The criterion makes a re-point succeeding on an unmatched patch-id a FAIL, so I built a scratch repo, established ground truth with git itself, and then checked whether the tool agreed — rather than trusting the tool to tell me what equivalence is.

Ground truth first: computed patch-ids independently with `git show <sha> | git patch-id --stable` for four commits — a shipped feature, a genuine relocation of that same change onto a different base (cherry-picked; patch-id confirmed IDENTICAL to the original), a commit with genuinely different content, and an empty commit (which produces no patch-id at all). Only then did I run the command:

    genuinely equivalent (patch-id match)   ACCEPTED   record moved to the new commit
    different content                       REFUSED    record unchanged
    empty commit (no patch-id computable)   REFUSED    record unchanged
    root commit                             REFUSED    record unchanged
    nonexistent ref                         REFUSED    record unchanged

No path re-points without a verified patch-id match. And the property that matters as much as the refusal: on every refusal the record is left exactly as it was — a failed re-point cannot half-write. The empty-commit case is the one I most expected to slip, because an absent patch-id is not an unequal one; it refuses, which means the guard is "both ids computed and equal" rather than "not unequal."

REQ 3's SECOND CRITERION — PIPEMAN CAN CLEAR IT ALONE. The failure this recovers from is an orphaned shipped commit after a rebase, and the recovery is one command Pipeman runs in its own session with no other role and no git surgery. That satisfies the transition-precondition rule this project has been applying since sprint 3, and it is the first new command in a while that was designed against that rule rather than checked against it afterwards.

REQ 4 — THE OTHER FAIL TRIGGER. Patch-id must not appear in the ship gate's path. Extracted the gate functions and checked each: `git_tree_hash_excluding` — absent; `differing_paths_excluding` — absent; `cmd_ship`'s tree comparison — absent. Enumerated every function in the file that mentions patch-id at all: `commit_patch_id`, `cmd_repoint`, `build_parser`. The equivalence notion stays quarantined in the recovery path and never touches the gate, which is the deliberate protection the requirement names.

================================================================
REQS 1 AND 2 — MET
================================================================

Req 1's split is behavioural, not wording. `workflows_configured_at()` runs `git ls-tree -r --name-only <commit> -- .github/workflows/` — the commit's own tree, local, no network, and scoped to the specific commit rather than to GitHub's current state. That distinction is the whole point and it is the reason the local check is better than `gh workflow list` here, not merely cheaper. Establishing that by testing `gh workflow list` directly rather than assuming it would do is the right order.

A CI-less project stays shippable: with no workflows in the tree, the no-runs-found case returns CI_STATUS_UNDETERMINABLE with the benign wording, exactly as before. Only "workflows exist AND no run was found for this commit" grades RED. The criterion warns that making CI-less projects unshippable would be worse than the defect — that outcome is avoided by construction.

Ship/reship parity: both functions contain one `check_ci_status` call, one RED branch and one UNDETERMINABLE branch. Same question, same answer, which is the standing rule from sprint 24's own Req 4 and is now inherited rather than re-decided.

Req 2 — the ordering is the requirement, and it holds: in `cmd_ship`'s body, `is_commit_reachable` appears at line 56 and `last_shipped_commit` is written at line 84. The check precedes the write, so a commit that is not on the branch being pushed never reaches the record at all.

REQ 5 / REQ 6 — package.json 0.2.1, one line. ALL SMOKE TESTS PASSED; ALL LAUNCHER TESTS PASSED, 199 OK; verify-tarball.sh PASSED, "Installed 0.2.1 (first install)".

================================================================
YOUR TWO QUESTIONS
================================================================

THE SCOPE QUESTION — the extra files are correct and I would have raised it if you had left them out. Team Assignments said "one file," but Req 3's own acceptance criterion says Pipeman must be able to clear the failure itself. A Python subcommand with no slash command is not something Pipeman can run in its own session as a sanctioned action — every other lifecycle transition in this framework is reached through `.claude/commands/`, and a recovery path reachable only by invoking the underlying script directly would fail the very criterion it exists to satisfy. The pipeman.md paragraph and the Quick Reference line are the same argument one step further: a command nobody is told about is the "capability nobody is prompted to invoke" problem this project already hit with the live-loop audit, which went unused for its entire first life for exactly that reason.

So: necessary, not scope creep. Flagging it rather than quietly widening the diff was still right — that is what makes it a decision Master Controller can ratify rather than discover. My read is it needs noting, not sign-off; if Master Controller disagrees, the thing to change is Team Assignments' wording, not the build.

THE MERGE-COMMIT LIMITATION — correctly identified and correctly left alone. `git patch-id` on a merge commit reads a combined diff, and what `git show` emits for a merge is not the same shape as for a normal commit, so the equivalence check's behaviour there is genuinely unknown rather than known-good. Two reasons not to touch it now: the incident this recovers from is a rebase orphaning a linear commit, and a merge commit is not what a rebase produces; and building a special case against untested behaviour is how sprint 26's fourteen unestablished claims happened. Naming it as untested in the code is the right disposition. If it ever matters, the failure mode is a refusal — the guard requires both ids computed and equal — so it fails closed, which is the safe direction for an unknown.

INFORMATIONAL, CARRIED: every allowlist entry other than git and npm remains inferred; the empty-string ownedRepository declaration still falls through silently; and who commits a QA1 verdict is still open from sprint 27, still Master Controller's.

RECOMMENDATION

Ship it. /sprint-dev-done 28, then Pipeman ships and publishes 0.2.1, then `verify-publish 28`.

And commit this verdict — sprint 27 shipped the notice that says so, and this is the first sprint audited under it.
commit=8fec6e6 | ci=green: 1 CI run(s) for 8fec6e603b0df753e3c308c6bd110114f7c3df06 all completed successfully with real steps executed.

PASS: PASS — round 1. Live-tested published npm 0.2.1 in scratch repos, plus read-only queries against this repository's real CI history. Environment: macOS Darwin arm64, 2026-09-09. No billed agent runs — every criterion here is a lifecycle-script or git property.

PROVENANCE
0.2.1 on the registry; dist-tags.latest 0.2.1; gitHead 8fec6e603b0df753e3c308c6bd110114f7c3df06 == last_shipped_commit; zero `reshipped` events. Content check per sprint 13's rule: all 62 published files byte-identical to `git show 8fec6e6:<path>`, MISMATCHED 0, tarball sha1 matches the registry's dist.shasum.

================================================================
CRITERION — THE CI CASES ARE GENUINELY DISTINCT: PASS. AND THIS CLOSES MY OWN SPRINT-24 GAP.
================================================================
My first attempt at this criterion proved nothing and I discarded it rather than report it: I built two scratch repos, one with a workflow file and one without, and both returned the identical "no git remotes found" message. The gh query fails before the workflow distinction is ever reached, so a repo with no remote cannot exercise this at all. `workflows_configured_at()` is a local `git ls-tree` check and needs no remote, but it only matters once gh can actually answer.

Constructed properly, against this repository's real history and real CI data, read-only:

  NO WORKFLOWS CONFIGURED (a commit predating .github/workflows/) -> status: undeterminable
    "no CI runs found for commit 236ba3a, and no CI is configured (.github/workflows/ is empty or
     absent in this commit's own tree) — benign, this project has no CI for this tool to see."

  WORKFLOWS CONFIGURED, ZERO RUNS FOR THIS COMMIT (1958d6b, an intermediate commit in a multi-commit
  push, so no run of its own) -> status: RED
    "workflows are configured (.github/workflows/ is non-empty in commit 1958d6b's own tree) but gh
     found zero runs for this exact commit — indistinguishable from a pipeline broken badly enough to
     never even start (a bad trigger condition, a workflow-syntax error, CI not yet caught up). Not
     treated as benign undeterminable: unlike 'no CI configured', this is exactly what a silently
     broken pipeline looks like."

  WORKFLOWS CONFIGURED, RUN SUCCEEDED -> status: green
    "1 CI run(s) ... all completed successfully with real steps executed."

Three states, three different verdicts, and the middle message tells a reader exactly why it is not being treated as the benign one. That is the criterion: treated differently, and distinguished to a reader.

THIS CLOSES A GAP I RECORDED AT SPRINT 24. There I wrote that the CI check's refusal branch was unexercised — "it will fire for real the first time a workflow misconfiguration produces a hollow green run, and nobody will have seen it work before that moment." It is no longer unexercised: I have now seen `check_ci_status` return **red** against real GitHub data. The trigger differs from the one I anticipated (zero runs rather than a hollow green run), so the hollow-green path specifically remains unobserved — but "red has never been produced by this code" is no longer true, and the branch that would block a ship demonstrably works.

================================================================
CRITERION — REPRODUCE THE ORPHANING AND RECOVER IT: PASS, BOTH DIRECTIONS
================================================================
Shipped a commit in a scratch repo, then rebased onto a moved base so the shipped commit became genuinely unreachable:
  shipped commit 0af4032; after rebase, `git merge-base --is-ancestor` reports NOT an ancestor of HEAD
  /sprint-liveqa correctly refused at that point — the recorded commit no longer describes anything
  on the branch

THE RECOVERY. The rebased equivalent (d97b8db) carries the same patch-id as the orphan, which I confirmed independently with `git patch-id --stable` on both before running anything: 5565009e840eaa0b on each.

  Sprint 1: last_shipped_commit re-pointed 0af4032... -> d97b8db...
    patch-id 5565009e840eaa0b... confirmed equal on both commits -- recorded in history.
    The ship gate's own tree comparison is untouched by this command (Req 4); only
    last_shipped_commit changed.

It prints the patch-id it matched on, records the re-point in history rather than silently rewriting the field, and states its own limits. A verdict then recorded normally against the recovered commit.

THE NEGATIVE TEST, which is what makes the tool safe rather than merely useful:
  ERROR: Sprint 1: 8d8bd2e... is NOT the same patch as d97b8db... (patch-id b83b41ff... !=
  5565009e...). Refusing to re-point -- this recovery restores a path for a commit relocated by a
  rebase; it is not a way to point a completed sprint at different content. No override.

Both patch-ids in the message, and the refusal names the distinction between recovery and redirection. A repoint that accepted any commit would be an override on a completed sprint wearing a recovery tool's name; this one cannot be used that way.

================================================================
CRITERION — THE SHIP GATE STILL REFUSES A REBASED COMMIT WITH A DIFFERENT TREE: PASS
================================================================
The repoint command claims in its own output that it leaves the ship gate's tree comparison untouched. That is a testable claim about a safety property, so I tested it rather than accept it.

Constructed a genuine rebase, not merely a divergent commit — my first attempt aborted on a dirty working tree and I redid it with the bookkeeping committed first, so that the audited commit was truly rebased away:
  audited state at 2010a93 (tree clean)
  after `git rebase` onto a divergent branch: HEAD b7d4dd0, and `merge-base --is-ancestor 2010a93 HEAD`
  reports NOT an ancestor — the audited commit is gone from the branch
  app.js content changed from "audited content" to "someone elses app.js"

  ERROR: Sprint 1: the commit being shipped doesn't match what QA1 audited (its file contents differ,
  even accounting for a rebase/squash/merge that preserves content). New changes landed after QA1's
  PASS need a fresh /sprint-qa1 audit before they can ship. No override.

Refused. The gate compares content, so a rebase that preserves content still ships (sprint 13's own relaxation, which I verified at sprint 24) while one that changes content does not — and adding a recovery path for orphaned commits did not weaken it.

================================================================
CORRECTIONS TO MY OWN METHOD THIS ROUND
================================================================
Three, all caught before reaching a verdict, recorded so the raw session isn't misread:
 - My first CI construction used two remote-less scratch repos and produced identical messages. It
   demonstrated nothing about the distinction; I discarded it and rebuilt against real CI data.
 - I invoked `repoint`; the subcommand is `repoint-shipped-commit`. A usage error of mine, not a
   defect.
 - My first rebase attempt aborted on a dirty tree, leaving a divergent commit rather than a rebased
   one. The gate refused either way, but "tree differs" and "rebased away" are different claims and
   the criterion asks for the second, so I rebuilt it.

================================================================
WHAT I OBSERVED VS ACCEPTED
================================================================
Every result here I produced directly against published 0.2.1. The patch-id equality underpinning the repoint I computed myself with `git patch-id --stable` before running the command, rather than reading the command's own report of it. The repoint's claim that it leaves the ship gate untouched I tested with a real rebase rather than accepted. Pipeman's report arrived mid-run and changed nothing.

QA1's now twice-flagged process gap — no role designated to commit its own verdict — is carried forward for the second time and is still Master Controller's. My position is unchanged from sprint 27: it is visible in this repository's own history, it applies to LiveQA as much as to QA1, and I am not resolving it by starting to commit unilaterally during a gate.

================================================================
RECOMMENDATION
================================================================
Ship-ready. The undeterminable CI case is now three cases with three verdicts, and the one that matters — workflows present, no run — is correctly treated as red rather than shrugged off, with a message that explains why it is not benign. The orphan recovery works on a patch-id match, records what it matched on, and refuses to become a redirection tool. The ship gate's own refusal survived the addition intact, which is the property most at risk when a recovery path is added next to a safety check.

One item carries forward from my own earlier gate rather than this one: the hollow-green CI case (a run that completes without executing steps) is still unobserved, though red as a verdict is no longer unexercised.

This PASS means the code is ready, not that anyone is authorized to close sprint 28.
